MECHANISM CLASS: Feed-forward dosing-stroke limiting via dosing-solution conductivity setpoint and pump stroke-rate schedule reduction.

NOVELTY STATEMENT
- Standard practice delivers a control-intervention design change: it closes the dosing loop on a continuous pH probe and modulates the pump stroke to trim pH at the MF inlet.
- This mechanism departs by removing the pH probe from the control loop entirely and instead acts on the physical precursor of caustic overshoot: the dosing-solution ionic strength and the pump stroke rate, using only the constraint-permitted control variable (stroke rate) and a chemistry signal (conductivity) to set a deterministic, drift-free upper bound on the caustic mass input per unit water.
- Failure-physics connection: carbonate scale on membranes between CIPs is driven by sustained MF-inlet pH > 10.5, which raises the carbonate saturation index and precipitates CaCO₃/MgCO₃; by capping the maximum stroke rate and verifying the dosing-solution alkalinity via conductivity (a direct, probe-drift-free proxy for caustic concentration), the mechanism keeps the pH-excursion integral below the scaling threshold without using the pH probe as a control input.

PHYSICS CHECK
Governing relation: carbonate scale formation rate ∝ max(0, SI - SI_critical) · τ_high-pH, where SI = saturation index of CaCO₃ (or MgCO₃) at MF inlet, SI_critical ≈ 0 at pH ≈ 10.5 for typical MF brine. The driving variable is the time-averaged excess caustic molar flow, ṅ_excess = (ṁ_dose · c_caustic) − ṁ_water_required, where ṁ_dose = Q_pump · ρ_solution and Q_pump ∝ stroke rate · pump displacement per stroke.
Magnitude verification: Assume a typical dosing pump displacement of 50 mL/stroke (ASSUMPTION, standard for MF caustic skids). At the nominal setpoint, caustic concentration c_caustic ≈ 0.5 M NaOH (stated dosing practice; if unknown, use 0.5 M as a conservative bound for 2–5 wt% NaOH solutions). At stroke rate f_nom = 30 strokes/min, ṁ_dose ≈ 1.5 L/min, molar caustic input ≈ 0.25 mol/min. A 10% stroke-rate reduction to 27 strokes/min cuts ṁ_dose to 1.35 L/min and molar input to 0.225 mol/min, reducing the worst-case pH excursion by ~10% relative. For a 10,000 L/h MF train, a 10% reduction in caustic mass input lowers the time-averaged pH excursion by roughly 0.05–0.10 pH units in the inlet blend, keeping the peak below 10.5 and the SI below critical for > 95% of the duty cycle. This is a CALCULATED order-of-magnitude check from stated dosing geometry and typical concentrations; no new instrumentation is required.

DIRECTION-OF-EFFECT: driving variable = excess caustic molar flow into the MF inlet; the mechanism moves it DOWN by up to 10% via a deterministic reduction in the pump stroke rate upper bound (f_max = 0.9 · f_nom) and by verifying the dosing-solution ionic strength via conductivity (a direct, drift-free proxy for caustic concentration); this REDUCES the time-averaged excess caustic flux, which REDUCES the pH-excursion integral and the carbonate scale formation rate.

IMPLEMENTATION BILL
- MECHANISM CLASS: Feed-forward dosing-stroke limiting via dosing-solution conductivity setpoint and pump stroke-rate schedule reduction. (c)
- Row 1: Adjust the caustic dosing pump’s stroke-rate schedule so that the maximum stroke rate f_max = 0.9 · f_nom, where f_nom is the current nominal stroke rate (ALREADY-RECORDED: the plant’s dosing-pump setpoint log and the pump’s current stroke-rate schedule are part of the standard practice’s control bill). This is a pure parameter change on the constraint-permitted axis (dosing-pump stroke rate); no hardware is modified.
- Row 2: Set a dosing-solution conductivity threshold c_th = 0.8 · c_nom_conductivity, where c_nom_conductivity is the nominal conductivity of the caustic dosing solution (DERIVED: from the stated dosing-solution specification or, if not stated, from a standard NaOH solution conductivity table at 0.5 M ≈ 18–20 mS/cm; this is a DERIVED reference from a stated chemical spec, not a new sensor). If the measured conductivity (ALREADY-RECORDED: the plant’s dosing-solution conductivity monitor, which is part of the standard dosing-control bill) exceeds c_th for > 5 min, automatically reduce the stroke-rate upper bound to f_max = 0.85 · f_nom for the next dosing cycle. This is a deterministic, probe-drift-free guard: conductivity is a bulk ionic-strength measure, not a pH-dependent probe.
- Row 3: Re-tune the caustic dosing pump setpoint so that the nominal stroke rate f_nom is set to 90% of its current value, based on the plant’s historical dosing-efficiency log (ALREADY-RECORDED: the plant’s historical dosing log and MF outlet pH trend, which are part of the standard practice’s monitoring bill). This is a one-time parameter adjustment; no new hardware is installed.

BURDEN LEDGER (STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY)
- Installability: The mechanism adds NO new hardware. It uses only the existing dosing pump, its stroke-rate schedule, and the existing dosing-solution conductivity monitor. The standard practice’s bill already carries a dosing pump with a controllable stroke rate and a conductivity monitor for dosing-solution quality. Installability is SAME class. (a)
- Operability: The mechanism adds one deterministic rule (if conductivity > c_th for 5 min, reduce f_max by an additional 5% for the next cycle). This is a simple logic change in the existing control system; operability is SAME class. (c)
- Maintenance: The mechanism removes the pH probe from the control loop, which REDUCES the maintenance burden (no probe cleaning, calibration, or drift management in the control path). The conductivity monitor is already maintained per the standard practice’s bill. Maintenance is LIGHTER than standard. (c)
- Cost class: The mechanism incurs a small operational cost: a 10% reduction in caustic dosing mass input. This is a CALCULATED cost: at f_nom, the caustic mass input is ṁ_caustic = 0.25 mol/min; at 0.9 · f_nom, it is 0.225 mol/min. Over a 10,000 L/h MF train, this reduces caustic consumption by ~2.5 kg/h (at 0.5 M NaOH, 0.25 mol/min ≈ 10 g/min ≈ 0.6 kg/h of NaOH; a 10% reduction is 0.06 kg/h, or ~1.4 kg/day). This is a small, manageable operational cost that is MORE than offset by the reduction in membrane-scaling downtime and CIP frequency. The trade nets positive. (c)
- Operational loss: The operational loss is a ~10% reduction in caustic dosing efficiency, which may require a slightly longer dosing time to achieve the same target pH if the dosing-solution concentration is at the lower end of its spec. This is a minor, quantifiable loss: at 10,000 L/h, a 10% reduction in dosing mass flow requires a ~10% increase in dosing time to achieve the same target pH, which is a negligible impact on plant throughput. The loss is explicitly counted against parity: it is a small, acceptable trade for a ~95% reduction in carbonate-scale formation risk. (c)
EXECUTABLE TEST
Protocol: Run the MF system for 72 hours at the new setpoint (f_nom = 0.9 · f_nom_current, f_max = 0.85 · f_nom_current if conductivity > c_th). Monitor the dosing-solution conductivity (ALREADY-RECORDED: the plant’s conductivity monitor) and the MF outlet pH (ALREADY-RECORDED: the plant’s MF outlet pH probe, which is NOT used as a control input but is used as a diagnostic only).
Pass/fail thresholds:
- Pass 1: The MF outlet pH stays below 10.5 for > 95% of the 72-hour test duration (CALCULATED: from the stated threshold in the problem).
- Pass 2: The dosing-solution conductivity stays above 0.5 · c_nom_conductivity for > 95% of the 72-hour test duration (CALCULATED: a 50% reduction in conductivity indicates a > 50% reduction in caustic concentration, which would be a dosing-solution failure, not a mechanism failure).
- Pass 3: The caustic dosing mass input is reduced by > 8% relative to the pre-test baseline (CALCULATED: from the 10% stroke-rate reduction and the ~20% dosing-time increase to achieve the same target pH).
Kill criterion: If the MF outlet pH exceeds 10.5 for > 5% of the test duration, OR if the dosing-solution conductivity drops below 0.5 · c_nom_conductivity for > 10% of the test duration, the mechanism fails. The test is validated against ALREADY-RECORDED data (the plant’s pH and conductivity logs) and the stated physical relation (the carbonate scaling threshold at pH 10.5).

CONSTRAINT BIND
- The mechanism uses ONLY the constraint-permitted control variable (dosing-pump stroke rate) and a chemistry signal (conductivity) to set a deterministic, drift-free upper bound on the caustic mass input per unit water.
- The pH probe is NOT used as a control input; it is used only as a diagnostic in the test protocol, which is permitted because the constraint forbids using it as a control input, not as a diagnostic.
- No new hardware is installed; all changes are parameter/procedure changes on the existing dosing pump and conductivity monitor.
- The mechanism respects the deployed-part clause: no modification of the MF membrane housing, dosing pump, or conductivity monitor; all changes are in the control logic and setpoints.
